Fast
FAST
v.
Old English fæstan, “to abstain from food.” Renders the Hebrew tsūm, “to abstain from food,” and the Greek nēsteuō, “to abstain from food for religious reasons.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To fast, in Scripture, is to abstain from food (and sometimes from drink and other ordinary goods) for a religious purpose—chiefly to humble oneself before God, to seek His face in earnest prayer, to mourn for sin, to wait on Him for guidance or deliverance, and to discipline the body that the soul may give itself more wholly to the LORD. The Bible records personal fasts (David fasted and prayed for his sick child; Daniel fasted three full weeks; Anna served God with fastings and prayers night and day), corporate fasts (the Day of Atonement; the fast of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months in Zechariah; the fast called by Jehoshaphat when the great enemy came against Judah), and the supreme fast of the Lord Jesus, who fasted forty days and forty nights in the wilderness before His ministry began. Christ assumes the practice of fasting in His disciples (when ye fast, not if ye fast) and corrects its abuses without abolishing the discipline; He explicitly answers the question why His disciples did not fast during His earthly presence with the prophecy that the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast in those days—that is, throughout the entire interval between His ascension and return. The apostolic church practiced fasting (Acts 13:2-3; 14:23); Paul ranks fastings among the marks of an apostolic ministry (2 Cor 6:5; 11:27); and the historic church has kept the discipline through every age. Isaiah 58 sets the most extended biblical theology of fasting at its sharpest: the fast God chooses is not mere abstinence with the spirit unchanged, but the fast that breaks every yoke, deals bread to the hungry, brings the poor into the house, and is matched by inward humbling and outward mercy. Fasting therefore is no work meriting reward; it is a posture, a deliberate emptying, by which the soul makes room for God where ordinary appetites have crowded Him out. Its primary register is humbling before God; its secondary effect, often surprising in its weight, is the recovery of spiritual hunger, the sharpening of prayer, and the loosening of the body’s tyrannical hold on the soul’s affections.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FAST as to abstain from food, beyond the usual time; to omit to take the usual meals, for a time; in a religious sense, to abstain from food for the mortifying of the body, or as a token of grief, sorrow and affliction.

expand to see more

FAST, v.i. — 1. To abstain from food, beyond the usual time; to omit to take the usual meals, for a time; as, to fast a day or a week. 2. To abstain from food voluntarily, for the mortification of the body or appetites, or as a token of grief, sorrow and affliction.

FAST, n. — Abstinence from food; properly, a total abstinence; voluntary forbearance of food, for the mortification of the body or appetites, or as a token of grief, mourning, sorrow, or affliction.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 6:16-18 — "Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast... But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret."

Isaiah 58:6-7 — "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry..."

Acts 13:2-3 — "As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them. And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away."

Matthew 9:15 — "And Jesus said unto them, Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Fasting is corrupted, on one side, by the modern evangelical neglect that has quietly dropped the discipline as Old Covenant or merely Catholic, against Christ’s own when ye fast—and on the other by the dietary-and-wellness rebranding that fasts for body composition, autophagy, and clarity rather than for the humbling of the soul before God.

expand to see more

Modern evangelicalism has, in much of its practice, quietly dropped the discipline of fasting—often by treating it as an Old Covenant practice not binding under the New, or as a residual Catholic-and-Orthodox liturgical habit foreign to gospel freedom. Christ’s own teaching refuses both excuses. He says when ye fast, not if ye fast; He announces that the bridegroom’s absence will be precisely the era in which His disciples fast; the apostles fast in Acts; Paul lists fastings among the marks of his ministry; the historic church has kept the discipline through every age. The recovery is not legalism but simple obedience to the assumed-practice of the New Testament church: regular fasting, often privately, as the Father in secret directs and rewards.

The contemporary culture has, meanwhile, rediscovered fasting in another key: intermittent fasting for body composition, prolonged fasts for autophagy and mental clarity, calorie restriction for longevity. The bodily benefits are real; the rebranding is the corruption. Biblical fasting is not body-optimization with a verse attached; it is the humbling of the soul before God for prayer, mourning, seeking, and the recovery of spiritual hunger—an essentially religious act with bodily incidentals. The believer who fasts only for the metabolic benefits has dropped the discipline’s actual purpose; the believer who fasts biblically often discovers the metabolic benefits as a secondary gift while the primary one—a soul humbled and a prayer sharpened—is being granted by the Father who sees in secret.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsūm (to abstain from food) and Greek nēsteuō (to fast)—the humbling of the soul before God by deliberate abstinence, assumed-practice of Christ’s disciples (when ye fast) and of the apostolic church.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsūm (H6684) — to abstain from food, to fast.

Hebrew tsōm (H6685) — a fast, a fasting (the noun).

Greek nēsteuō (G3522) — to fast, abstain from food for religious reasons.

Greek nēsteia (G3521) — fasting (the noun); 2 Cor 6:5; 11:27.

Usage

"Christ said when ye fast, not if ye fast—the discipline is the assumed-practice of His disciples throughout the bridegroom’s absence."

"Intermittent fasting for body composition is bodily; biblical fasting is the humbling of the soul before God, with metabolic benefits as secondary gifts."
